practice_questions.text:
Which life stage covers the age range 11 to 19 years?
A) Childhood
B) Adolescence
C) Adulthood
D) Later adulthood
practice_questions.marks: B) Adolescence [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the age range for later adulthood.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: 65 years and over (accept: 65+). No other range accepted.

practice_questions.text: Describe one intellectual milestone a child in the childhood life stage (3–10 years) might reach.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying a relevant intellectual milestone. 1 mark for a qualifying detail.
Accept:
• Vocabulary expands rapidly (1) — for example, growing from around 200 words at age 2 to several thousand by age 7 (1).
• Children begin to read and write (1) — they develop the ability to decode letters and form sentences as formal schooling begins (1).
• Children develop theory of mind (1) — the ability to understand that others have different thoughts and perspectives from their own (1).
Do not credit one-word answers with no qualifying detail.

practice_questions.text: Give two physical changes that typically occur during later adulthood.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for two genuinely different physical changes:
• Bone density decreases, increasing the risk of fractures (1)
• Muscle strength reduces (1)
• Sensory abilities (sight, hearing) may decline (1)
• Immune function weakens (1)
• Processing speed slows (1 — accept if described as physical)
Maximum 2 marks. Do not credit near-identical points.

practice_questions.text: Explain why knowledge of life-stage milestones is important for health and social care practitioners.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks. Requires a reason using 'because', 'therefore', or 'this means that'.
• Practitioners need to know what typical development looks like (1) because this allows them to recognise when an individual is not meeting expected milestones (1) and therefore refer them to the appropriate support services in good time (1).
• Accept other valid chains provided they give a reason and a consequence.

practice_questions.text: Priya Osei is 74 years old and lives alone since her husband died two years ago. She attends a day centre three times a week. She has recently been diagnosed with osteoporosis and has also noticed that she struggles to remember recent conversations. Using the PIES framework, analyse how Priya's physical and intellectual development in later adulthood may be affecting her overall health and well-being.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Detailed PIES analysis that chains physical and intellectual development changes to their emotional and social consequences. Directly and consistently references Priya's circumstances (osteoporosis, memory difficulties, bereavement, day centre).

Secure (5–6): Clear PIES coverage for at least three domains with generally accurate application to Priya. Some chaining between domains. May not chain all four domains fully.

Developing (3–4): Accurate points but listed rather than chained. Limited reference to Priya specifically.

Emerging (1–2): Basic points with minimal PIES structure and little application to the scenario.

Indicative content:
• Physical (osteoporosis): reduced bone density increases fracture risk — Priya may fear falls, limiting her mobility and participation in day-centre activities.
• Physical chain: reduced mobility → less social contact → increased loneliness and isolation (social and emotional impact).
• Intellectual (memory difficulties): struggling to recall recent conversations may indicate early cognitive decline, affecting Priya’s ability to follow discussions at the day centre.
• Intellectual chain: memory decline → reduced confidence in social interactions → withdrawal and lower self-esteem (emotional and social impact).
• Emotional: bereavement from husband’s death compounds later-adulthood emotional challenges; emotional wellbeing is affected by both physical vulnerability and cognitive changes.
• Social: the day centre is a protective factor — it provides peer contact and routine, partially countering the social risks of living alone in later adulthood.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes 'active participation' in health and social care?
A) Ensuring every individual can access services on an equal basis
B) An individual's ability to adapt to unexpected challenges
C) Involving individuals in decisions about their own care and lives
D) How a person thinks about and evaluates themselves
practice_questions.marks: C) Involving individuals in decisions about their own care and lives [1 mark]. A describes inclusion; B describes resilience; D describes self-concept.

practice_questions.text: Identify two characteristics of inclusion in a health and social care setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct, accurate characteristics (max 2). Acceptable answers include: equal access for all individuals regardless of need [1]; removing physical, communicative or attitudinal barriers [1]; ensuring no individual is shut out of services [1]; reasonable adjustments made for different needs [1]. Two near-identical points (e.g. 'equal access' and 'fair access') score 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by 'resilience' in a health and social care context.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying the core meaning (ability to adapt to life's unexpected challenges); 1 mark for a reason using 'because' or 'therefore' (e.g. because it allows individuals to manage social disadvantage, family or workplace difficulties); 1 mark for a developed application or example (e.g. therefore a care worker can support a service user to build coping strategies rather than creating long-term dependence on services).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a practitioner at a day centre for adults with physical disabilities could promote active participation for the individuals they support.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. 2 marks for describing active participation accurately (individuals having a say in decisions about their care and daily activities) with reference to the day centre setting. 2 marks for a specific, plausible example with detail — e.g. holding a weekly group where service users vote on activities [1], then using individual key-worker meetings to record each person's personal preferences and reviewing these monthly [1]. Answers that describe inclusion instead of active participation are awarded a maximum of 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how self-concept is linked to resilience for individuals who use health and social care services.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Identifies the link between self-concept (how individuals think about and value themselves) and resilience (adapting to adversity) with developed reasoning from at least two angles. Example content: a positive self-concept supports resilience because an individual who believes in their own capabilities is better placed to adapt when challenges arise; conversely, a negative self-concept (e.g. low self-esteem resulting from abuse or exclusion) can undermine resilience by making the individual feel unable to cope. May also explore the role of practitioner support in building both simultaneously. Uses 'because', 'therefore', 'this means that'.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies the link with some development; may address only one direction of the relationship.

Developing (2 marks): Names both concepts but offers limited explanation of the connection.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one concept correctly with little or no link to the other.

practice_questions.text:
Fatima is 15 years old and lives in a residential children's home. She has experienced significant family disruption and has low self-esteem. She rarely joins in group activities and says she does not want to be involved in any decisions about her care.

Analyse how the key worker at the home could use active participation, inclusion and an understanding of resilience to support Fatima's well-being.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Chains the analysis across all three concepts with reference to Fatima's specific circumstances. Example content: Active participation — the key worker could begin with small, low-pressure choices (e.g. what to eat for breakfast) rather than large care-plan decisions, because Fatima's low self-esteem means being asked to make major decisions immediately could feel overwhelming, therefore gradually building her sense of agency. Inclusion — offering one-to-one alternatives to group activities means Fatima is not excluded simply because of her preference, because inclusion requires removing barriers not insisting on conformity. Resilience — by praising small achievements and reflecting on past difficulties Fatima has managed, the key worker helps her recognise her own capacity to adapt, because resilience is built through experience of overcoming adversity with support. Candidate shows how the three concepts interact: active participation builds agency, agency supports resilience, inclusion ensures Fatima feels valued and her self-concept improves.

Secure (5–6 marks): Addresses all three concepts with mostly developed reasoning; some reference to Fatima's circumstances.

Developing (3–4 marks): Addresses two concepts with some development; links to Fatima's circumstances are partial.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Names concepts with little development or application.

practice_questions.text:
Which reflex causes a newborn baby's fingers to close around an object placed in their palm?
A) Rooting reflex
B) Moro reflex
C) Grasp reflex
D) Startle reflex
practice_questions.marks: C) Grasp reflex [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two physical changes that typically occur in boys during puberty.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for two genuinely different physical changes in boys:
• Growth of the testes/penis (1)
• Development of pubic, facial, or body hair (1)
• Voice deepening/voice breaking (1)
• Growth of muscle mass (1)
• Growth spurt (1)
Do not credit near-identical points.

practice_questions.text: Describe one difference between gross motor skills and fine motor skills, using an example of each.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for a correct distinction. 1 mark for a relevant example of each:
• Gross motor skills involve large muscle groups (1) — e.g. running, jumping, crawling (1).
• Fine motor skills involve small muscles of the hands and fingers (1) — e.g. pincer grasp, using scissors, holding a pencil (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain two physical effects of the menopause on a woman's health.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks. Requires explanation using 'because', 'therefore', or 'this means that'.
• The menopause reduces oestrogen (1), which causes bone density to fall (1), therefore increasing the risk of osteoporosis and fractures (1).
• Accept also: hot flushes caused by hormonal changes; sleep disturbance; end of menstruation/fertility.
Award 1 mark for a named effect; up to 2 further marks for developed explanation and consequence.

practice_questions.text: Describe, with examples, how a person's physical development changes between early adulthood and later adulthood.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. 2 marks for adulthood, 2 marks for later adulthood. Each requires a feature plus an applied example.
Adulthood:
• Physical strength peaks in the mid-twenties (1) — e.g. a 25-year-old athlete will have faster reaction times and higher muscle strength than they will at 60 (1).
Later adulthood:
• Muscle mass declines more rapidly (sarcopenia) and bone density falls (1) — e.g. a 70-year-old is at higher risk of hip fractures from falls than a 30-year-old (1).
• Accept other valid applied examples from a care setting context.

practice_questions.text: Mr Darius Ayad is 71 years old. He lives in a residential care home and has recently been diagnosed with osteoporosis following a minor fall. He also has difficulty hearing conversations in group activities and has been prescribed hearing aids. Using the PIES framework, analyse how the physical changes of later adulthood are affecting Mr Ayad's overall health and well-being.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Detailed analysis chaining physical changes to their emotional and social consequences, with consistent reference to Mr Ayad's circumstances (osteoporosis, hearing loss, residential care setting).

Secure (5–6): Clear PIES coverage for at least three domains with accurate application to Mr Ayad. Some chaining. May not fully develop all four domains.

Developing (3–4): Accurate points listed but not chained. Limited reference to Mr Ayad.

Emerging (1–2): Basic points with little PIES structure.

Indicative content:
• Physical: osteoporosis from reduced bone density increases fracture risk — Mr Ayad may fear further falls and restrict movement. Hearing loss reduces ability to follow conversations in group activities.
• Physical chain: restricted mobility → reduced participation in activities → reduced social contact and intellectual stimulation.
• Emotional: fear of falling can create anxiety; hearing difficulties may cause frustration or embarrassment in social situations.
• Social: hearing loss in group settings leads to social withdrawal — Mr Ayad may stop joining communal activities, increasing isolation even within the care home.
• Intellectual: reduced engagement in group activities means less cognitive stimulation, which can accelerate cognitive decline.
• Protective factor: residential care home setting provides support with daily tasks, monitoring of fall risk, and social opportunities even with physical limitations.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is one of the twelve factors that can affect self-concept?
A) Resilience
B) Active participation
C) Unconscious bias
D) Well-being
practice_questions.marks: C) Unconscious bias [1 mark]. Resilience, active participation and well-being are related concepts but are not listed among the twelve factors affecting self-concept.

practice_questions.text: Give two ways in which social media can negatively affect an individual's self-concept.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct, accurate points (max 2). Acceptable answers: constant comparison to filtered/curated images leads to feelings of inadequacy [1]; relying on likes and followers as a measure of self-worth makes self-concept unstable and dependent on external approval [1]; cyberbullying via social media platforms damages self-esteem [1]. Two near-identical points score 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: Explain how stereotyping and discrimination can negatively affect a person's self-concept.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for identifying the effect (experiencing stereotyping or discrimination leads to lower self-esteem / negative self-concept); 1 mark for a developed reason using 'because' (e.g. because repeated messages that a person is inferior or 'less than' are internalised over time); 1 mark for a further development or example (e.g. therefore the individual begins to believe these negative messages about themselves, which affects their emotional well-being and their willingness to engage with education, employment or social opportunities).

practice_questions.text: Describe two strategies a key worker at a residential care home could use to help an older adult develop resilience following a bereavement.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per strategy, applied to the care home context. Example: Recognising personal strengths and qualities (2 marks) — 1 mark for naming the strategy; 1 mark for describing a specific key-worker action with reference to the care home setting (e.g. the key worker meets regularly with the resident to discuss a skill or quality they have demonstrated that week, such as showing patience during a physiotherapy session, so that the resident begins to recognise their own capabilities). Setting realistic goals (2 marks) — 1 mark for naming the strategy; 1 mark for a specific example (e.g. agreeing with the resident that they will attend one group activity per week rather than expecting full re-engagement with social life immediately). Other strategies accepted with equivalent development.

practice_questions.text: Discuss how two factors affecting self-concept can interact to produce a compounded negative effect on an individual's well-being.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Selects two distinct factors from the twelve and explains each separately, then shows how they interact to produce a compounded effect. Uses 'because', 'therefore', 'this means that'. Example content: Income affects self-concept negatively because poverty restricts the individual's access to resources associated with social acceptance (clothing, activities, food) [1], therefore the individual may feel different from peers and develop low self-esteem [1]. Education interacts with income: a person from a low-income background may attend a school with fewer resources, limiting their academic achievement [1], which reduces their sense of capability and reinforces a negative self-concept [1]. Together, low income and limited educational achievement create a compounding effect — each factor makes the negative impact of the other worse, reducing the individual's overall sense of worth and future prospects [2].

Secure (3–4 marks): Addresses both factors with some development; the interaction is identified but not fully explored.

Developing (2 marks): Describes both factors in isolation without showing how they interact.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one factor with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Kolade is 17 years old and has recently left care. He struggled at school, has a difficult relationship with his family, and has low self-esteem. He is now living independently in a supported housing placement. His support worker wants to help him develop a more positive self-concept and build resilience.

Evaluate how effectively the six resilience strategies could support Kolade's well-being in his current situation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9–10 marks): Selects at least four of the six strategies, evaluates each with specific reference to Kolade's circumstances (care leaver, low self-esteem, difficult family relationships, independent living), and makes a balanced overall judgement about effectiveness. Example content: Self-reflection — supports Kolade because care leavers have often managed significant adversity; reflecting on past difficulties he has overcome provides evidence of his own resilience [positive]; however, if reflection focuses primarily on failure (school struggles, family breakdown) without skilled facilitation by the support worker, it could reinforce negative self-concept [limitation]. Recognising personal strengths — highly relevant given Kolade's low self-esteem; the support worker's role is to identify and name strengths he cannot yet see himself [positive]. Participating in new activities — supported housing often provides opportunities for this; each successful new experience adds to Kolade's evidence of capability [positive]; however, anxiety or past rejection may make trying new things threatening [limitation]. Setting realistic goals — essential for Kolade, who may have experienced only unachievable targets in school; small, achievable milestones (e.g. attending college interview) protect self-concept [positive]. Conclusion: all six strategies have potential, but their effectiveness depends on the quality of the support worker relationship and Kolade's readiness to engage. The strategies work best in combination, not isolation.

Secure (6–8 marks): Addresses most strategies with relevant reference to Kolade; some evaluation of effectiveness.

Developing (3–5 marks): Describes some strategies with limited evaluation; application to Kolade is partial.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Names one or two strategies with minimal application.

practice_questions.text:
According to the WHO definition, health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and:
A) The presence of all essential nutrients in the body
B) Not merely the absence of disease or infirmity
C) Freedom from stress and anxiety at all times
D) A high level of fitness and regular exercise
practice_questions.marks: B) Not merely the absence of disease or infirmity [1 mark]. This is the verbatim WHO definition from 1948. All other options are plausible but incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Identify the organisation responsible for the definition of health used in this qualification.
practice_questions.marks: The World Health Organization / WHO [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'illness' in health and social care.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core meaning (the personal / subjective feeling or experience of being unwell); 1 mark for a relevant qualifying detail (e.g. illness is personal to the individual and may not always match a medically identified disease; a person can experience illness without a diagnosable disease being present).

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between illness and disease, using an example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining illness (the subjective personal experience of feeling unwell); 1 mark for defining disease (an objective clinical condition with specific identifiable signs and symptoms); 1 mark for an accurate example that illustrates the difference (e.g. a person may feel genuinely fatigued and unwell — illness — but medical tests find no identifiable condition — no disease present; or a person with early-stage hypertension has a diagnosed disease but feels completely well in themselves — disease without illness).

practice_questions.text: Discuss how the WHO definition of health is different from simply being free from illness or disease.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Identifies that the WHO definition is holistic (covers physical, mental and social dimensions); explains that 'not merely the absence of disease' means health is a positive state, not just the lack of something negative; discusses what this means in practice for health promotion and care. May also explore the high bar set by 'complete' well-being and whether it is achievable. Uses developed reasoning with 'because', 'therefore'.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies the holistic nature and makes some comparison with 'just not being ill'; some development.

Developing (2 marks): Notes that health includes mental and social dimensions but does not fully develop the argument.

Emerging (1 mark): Quotes part of the definition without explanation.

practice_questions.text:
Nadia is 58 years old. She has been feeling exhausted, low in mood and unable to concentrate for several months. Her GP has run blood tests which have come back clear. Nadia feels that something is wrong but has been told she is 'medically fine.'

Using the definitions of health, illness and well-being, analyse how Nadia's situation demonstrates the complexity of assessing an individual's health and well-being.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Applies all three definitions accurately to Nadia's circumstances. Illness — Nadia is clearly experiencing illness: the subjective feeling of being unwell is present (exhaustion, low mood, poor concentration); the fact that blood tests are clear does not mean illness is absent, because illness is personal and subjective [1+1]. Disease — no diagnosable disease has been found, which illustrates that illness can exist without disease [1]. Health — Nadia does not meet the WHO definition of complete physical, mental and social well-being: her mental well-being (mood, concentration) is affected, and social well-being may also be compromised if she is withdrawing from activities [1+1]. Well-being — Nadia is not thriving or experiencing high life satisfaction; her ability to manage stress and sense of purpose appear diminished [1]. Analysis chains the concepts: the complexity is that traditional clinical measures of health (blood tests) do not capture Nadia's subjective experience of illness or her reduced well-being; a holistic approach, as implied by the WHO definition, would take her experience seriously alongside the test results [1+1].

Secure (5–6 marks): Applies at least two definitions with mostly accurate analysis linked to Nadia.

Developing (3–4 marks): Applies one definition with limited reference to Nadia.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Names one definition with minimal application.

practice_questions.text:
Which Piaget stage is characterised by the ability to think logically about concrete events but not yet about abstract or hypothetical situations?
A) Sensorimotor
B) Pre-operational
C) Concrete operational
D) Formal operational
practice_questions.marks: C) Concrete operational [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Name the four stages of Piaget's theory of cognitive development, in the correct order.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for all four stages in the correct order:
Sensorimotor → pre-operational → concrete operational → formal operational.
No mark if order is incorrect or a stage is missing.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the pre-operational stage of cognitive development.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for a correct feature; 1 mark for a qualifying detail or example.
• Egocentric thinking (1) — the child assumes everyone else sees and experiences the world in the same way they do (1).
• Lack of conservation (1) — the child believes that changing the appearance of a quantity (e.g. pouring water into a different shaped glass) changes the amount (1).
• Use of symbols/language to represent objects (1) — children in this stage use words and images to stand for objects they know, allowing more complex play (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how a child's moral reasoning changes as they move from Kohlberg's pre-conventional level to the conventional level.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
• At the pre-conventional level, a child makes moral decisions based on self-interest (1) — for example, deciding not to steal because they fear punishment rather than because it harms others (1).
• At the conventional level, moral decisions are based on social rules and the expectations of others (1), therefore the individual wants to follow laws and be seen as a good member of society rather than just avoiding personal consequences (1).
Maximum 3 marks. Reason word required for the third mark.

practice_questions.text: Describe, with an example, how a practitioner working in an early years setting could apply their knowledge of Piaget's concrete operational stage to support a child's learning.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. 2 marks for the description; 2 marks for the applied example.
• The concrete operational stage (ages 7–11) means children can think logically about real, observable events but struggle with abstract concepts (1) — therefore a practitioner should use hands-on, practical activities rather than purely verbal or abstract instruction (1).
• For example, a teaching assistant could use physical counting objects to help a child understand maths rather than presenting sums in the abstract (1), because the child can reason logically about what they can see and manipulate directly (1).

practice_questions.text:
Theo is 9 years old and lives in a foster placement. His foster carer has noticed he finds it difficult to see other people's points of view during arguments with other children and becomes frustrated when rules change without explanation. His school has asked a learning support assistant to work with him.

Using Piaget's stages of cognitive development, analyse how Theo's cognitive development might be influencing his behaviour, and explain what this means for how the learning support assistant should support him.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Accurate identification of Theo's likely Piaget stage (concrete operational, possibly transitioning from pre-operational given some egocentric tendencies). Detailed analysis linking stage features to described behaviours. Clear, specific advice for the learning support assistant grounded in Piaget's framework. Consistent reference to Theo's circumstances (foster placement, arguments, rule changes).

Secure (5–6): Accurate stage identification with reasonable analysis and some practical advice for the practitioner. Limited development of the emotional/social implications.

Developing (3–4): Some accurate Piaget content but analysis descriptive rather than applied to Theo. Advice is generic.

Emerging (1–2): Basic Piaget recall with little application.

Indicative content:
• At 9, Theo is in the concrete operational stage (7–11) — he can think logically about concrete events but may still show some egocentric tendencies from the pre-operational stage.
• Difficulty seeing others' viewpoints links to residual egocentric thinking — he interprets situations from his own perspective, which can appear as selfishness but is a cognitive characteristic of this developmental stage.
• Frustration at rule changes links to the concrete operational child's need for clear, consistent, observable rules — abstract or frequently changing rules are cognitively difficult to process.
• The learning support assistant should use clear, step-by-step explanations of rules and consequences (concrete, not abstract), role-play activities to develop perspective-taking, and consistent routines that give Theo cognitive predictability.
• The foster placement context is relevant — children who have experienced disruption may show developmental delays; the practitioner should not assume Theo is operating at the top of the concrete operational stage.

practice_questions.text:
Which theorist designed the 'Strange Situation' to measure the quality of attachment between an infant and their caregiver?
A) John Bowlby
B) Mary Ainsworth
C) Albert Bandura
D) Jean Piaget
practice_questions.marks: B) Mary Ainsworth [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two attachment types identified by Ainsworth in the Strange Situation.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for any two of the three correct attachment types:
• Secure attachment (1)
• Insecure-avoidant attachment (1)
• Insecure-resistant (ambivalent) attachment (1)
Do not credit near-identical descriptions of the same type.

practice_questions.text: Explain what Bowlby meant by 'monotropy' in his attachment theory.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
• Monotropy is the idea that infants form one primary attachment that is qualitatively different from all other relationships (1).
• This primary caregiver (often but not always the mother) provides an internal working model (1) — a mental template of relationships that shapes expectations of future relationships throughout the individual's life (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how Albert Bandura's social learning theory could explain how an adolescent picks up a new behaviour from their peer group, using an example.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. 2 marks for description of social learning; 2 marks for an applied example.
• Bandura argued that behaviour is learned through observation and modelling — watching others and imitating their behaviour, especially if the model is admired or rewarded (1). Vicarious reinforcement occurs when an individual imitates behaviour after seeing another person rewarded for it (1).
• For example, a 14-year-old who observes peers gaining social approval for wearing a particular style of clothing is likely to imitate it (1), because the social reward (acceptance, admiration) acts as vicarious reinforcement even though the individual was not directly rewarded themselves (1).

practice_questions.text: Jaylen is 13 months old and lives with his mother and grandmother. His key-worker at nursery has observed that when his mother drops him off, Jaylen cries but is quickly reassured by a familiar key-worker. When his mother returns at the end of the day, Jaylen moves eagerly towards her and is quickly settled and returns to playing. Using Ainsworth's attachment types, discuss what Jaylen's behaviour suggests about his attachment, and explain what this means for his future social and emotional development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Correctly identifies Jaylen's behaviour as consistent with secure attachment. Discusses both what this predicts for positive future development AND acknowledges that attachment is not destiny (other life experiences also matter). Consistently references Jaylen's specific circumstances and care setting context.

Secure (3–4): Correct identification of secure attachment with some discussion of implications for future development. May not fully address counter-considerations.

Developing (2): Identifies the correct attachment type with limited discussion.

Emerging (1): Names an attachment type with no discussion or limited accuracy.

Indicative content:
• Jaylen's behaviour — distress at separation but easy comfort on reunion and return to play — is the defining profile of secure attachment (Ainsworth's Strange Situation).
• Secure attachment suggests Jaylen has a consistent, responsive primary caregiver; his internal working model (Bowlby) will be one of trust and reliability.
• Predicted positive outcomes: tends toward higher self-esteem, more trusting peer relationships in childhood, better capacity for intimate partnerships in adulthood.
• The role of the nursery key-worker as a secondary attachment figure is also relevant — a secure base in the nursery setting supports separation.
• Counter-consideration: attachment type is not fixed — adverse life experiences (bereavement, family breakdown) can alter the trajectory; positive relationships later can also partially compensate for early insecure attachment.

practice_questions.text: Nadia Osei is 15 years old. She attends a pupil referral unit after being excluded from her secondary school. Her early years records indicate she spent 18 months in foster care between ages 1 and 3 after her birth family could not care for her. She currently has no stable friendship group and finds it difficult to trust adults in authority. Using your knowledge of Bowlby's attachment theory and Bandura's social learning theory, analyse how Nadia's early experiences and current peer environment may be affecting her social and emotional development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Detailed analysis drawing on both Bowlby and Bandura with accurate theoretical content. Chains early attachment disruption to Nadia's current difficulties with trust and peer relationships. Addresses the social learning dimension (pupil referral unit peer environment, role models). Consistently applied to Nadia's circumstances throughout.

Secure (5–6): Accurate use of both theories with clear links to Nadia. Some chaining. May not fully integrate both theories.

Developing (3–4): Accurate theoretical content but applied descriptively rather than analytically. May address only one theory.

Emerging (1–2): Basic theoretical recall with minimal application to Nadia.

Indicative content:
Bowlby application:
• Foster care from ages 1–3 falls within Bowlby's critical period (0–3 years) for attachment formation. Disruption to the primary attachment during this period is associated with lasting emotional and social consequences.
• Nadia's difficulty trusting adults is consistent with Bowlby's concept of the internal working model — her early experience of inconsistent or disrupted caregiving may have produced a working model of adults as unreliable or threatening.
• This affects her emotional wellbeing (inability to form secure bonds) and social development (cannot build stable friendships, which require trust).
Bandura application:
• The pupil referral unit peer environment is significant. If the dominant peer models demonstrate anti-social behaviour, poor academic engagement, or conflict with authority figures, Nadia is likely to observe and imitate these behaviours through vicarious reinforcement — especially if those behaviours are rewarded with peer status or approval.
• Positive role models from practitioners in the unit (key workers, mentors) can provide alternative modelling — if Nadia observes consistent, trustworthy adult behaviour, social learning theory suggests this can begin to counteract her negative internal working model.
Integration:
• Bowlby explains WHY Nadia struggles with trust (disrupted early attachment); Bandura explains HOW her current environment shapes what behaviours she is learning now. Both frameworks point to the importance of stable, consistent, trusted adult relationships in the pupil referral unit as the primary mechanism for supporting her recovery.

practice_questions.text:
Which blood pressure reading indicates hypertension in an adult?
A) 110/70 mmHg
B) 120/80 mmHg
C) 130/85 mmHg
D) 145/95 mmHg
practice_questions.marks: D) 145/95 mmHg [1 mark]. Hypertension is defined as 140/90 mmHg or above. Options A and B are within the healthy range; option C is slightly elevated but does not meet the clinical hypertension threshold.

practice_questions.text: A service user weighs 78 kg and is 1.60 m tall. Calculate their BMI and state which category they fall into.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct calculation method and answer: 1.60 × 1.60 = 2.56; 78 ÷ 2.56 = 30.5 (accept 30–31 depending on rounding) [1]. 1 mark for correctly identifying the category as obese (BMI ≥30) [1]. A correct method with an arithmetic error scores 1 mark. Simply writing '30.5' without identifying the category scores 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: Give two contributing factors that a health professional should consider when interpreting an individual's BMI reading.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct contributing factors from the four named ones (max 2): age [1]; sex [1]; lifestyle (e.g. diet, physical activity levels) [1]; environment (e.g. access to green spaces, local food options) [1]. Two near-identical answers (e.g. 'poor diet' and 'eating too much') score 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: Explain why peak flow results cannot be interpreted using a single universal 'normal' range.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that expected peak flow varies by individual characteristics (age, height, sex); 1 mark for a reason using 'because' (e.g. because a taller adult male has a greater lung capacity than a child, so the same reading could be normal for one person and abnormal for another); 1 mark for a practical implication or example (e.g. therefore practitioners always compare a reading to the individual's personal best or a predicted value based on their age, height and sex, rather than a fixed range).

practice_questions.text:
The table below shows three physical indicator readings for Marcus (46 years old, male, desk job, smokes 10 cigarettes per day):

Blood pressure: 148/96 mmHg
Resting pulse rate: 88 bpm
BMI: 31.2

Analyse what this data suggests about Marcus's health, using your knowledge of normal values and contributing factors.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Addresses all three indicators, compares each to normal values, correctly classifies each, and chains analysis through at least two contributing factors linked to Marcus's specific circumstances. Blood pressure: 148/96 mmHg is above 140/90 — hypertension [1]; this is a significant risk for heart disease and stroke [1]. Resting pulse: 88 bpm is within the 60–100 bpm normal range for adults, though at the upper end; Marcus's sedentary job and smoking may mean his cardiovascular fitness is poor [1]. BMI: 31.2 places Marcus in the obese category (≥30) [1]. Contributing factors: age (46 — metabolic rate slows in middle adulthood, making weight gain more likely) [1]; lifestyle (smoking raises blood pressure and reduces cardiovascular fitness; sedentary desk job reduces calorie expenditure) [1]; environment (desk job = prolonged sitting; may have limited access to exercise during working day) [1]. Analysis chains: his elevated BMI and sedentary lifestyle contribute to his high blood pressure; smoking compounds this by reducing arterial flexibility. A practitioner would not look at readings in isolation but recognise that multiple indicators suggesting poor cardiovascular health represent a compounded risk [1].

Secure (5–6 marks): Addresses at least two indicators correctly with some contributing factor analysis linked to Marcus.

Developing (3–4 marks): Addresses one or two indicators; limited contributing factor analysis.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Identifies a reading as high or low with minimal explanation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the usefulness of BMI as a physical indicator of health for health professionals working in a primary care setting.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9–10 marks): Balanced evaluation identifying specific strengths of BMI (easy to calculate from height and weight, provides a consistent basis for comparison across populations, linked to clear risk thresholds for conditions such as type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease, widely used and understood by practitioners) alongside specific limitations (does not distinguish between fat mass and muscle mass so may overestimate risk in muscular individuals; does not indicate fat distribution — waist-to-hip ratio is better for this; expected ranges may not apply equally across ethnic groups; does not capture mental, social or other dimensions of health; a single reading is less informative than a trend). Evaluates in context of primary care: a GP may use BMI as a quick initial screening tool but would combine it with other indicators (blood pressure, waist-to-hip ratio, lifestyle information). Reaches a reasoned conclusion: BMI is a useful starting point but should never be the only measure used, because its limitations can lead to misclassification. An effective evaluation gives specific examples and avoids purely listing pros and cons without linking them.

Secure (6–8 marks): Addresses most strengths and limitations with some development and a conclusion.

Developing (3–5 marks): Notes some strengths and limitations with limited development.

Emerging (1–2 marks): One-sided or very general response with no conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of a life factor (rather than a lifestyle choice)?
A) Choosing to follow a vegan diet
B) Deciding to take up regular swimming
C) Living in an overcrowded home in an area with high air pollution
D) Choosing to smoke cigarettes
practice_questions.marks: C) Living in an overcrowded home in an area with high air pollution [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two types of abuse identified in the specification.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for any two correctly named abuse types from the spec list:
• Physical, emotional, sexual, verbal, neglect, coercive control, financial (any two for the mark).

practice_questions.text: Give two ways that living in poverty can negatively affect a child's development.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for two genuinely different effects:
• Poor nutrition affecting physical growth and brain development (1)
• Damp or overcrowded housing increasing respiratory illness (1)
• Limited access to educational resources, affecting intellectual development (1)
• The stress of financial insecurity affecting emotional wellbeing (1)
• Reduced social participation due to inability to afford activities or clothing (1)
Do not credit near-identical points.

practice_questions.text: Explain how an authoritative parenting style can positively affect a child's social and emotional development.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
• Authoritative parenting combines high warmth with clear, explained rules (1).
• This means a child develops a secure sense of what is expected of them (1), therefore they are more likely to develop high self-esteem and good social skills because they feel valued and supported while learning appropriate boundaries (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe, with an example, how poor access to services can affect an individual's health and development across the lifespan.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. 2 marks for description; 2 marks for applied example.
• Access to services is a life factor affecting whether individuals can benefit from immunisations, mental health support, early years provision, or day centres (1). Where access is limited by geography, cost, or language barriers, individuals cannot receive the support that would maintain or improve their health (1).
• For example, an older adult in a rural area who has no transport and no nearby day centre may become severely socially isolated (1), meaning they lose regular social contact and stimulation that would support both their emotional and intellectual wellbeing (1).

practice_questions.text:
Sienna Okafor is 8 years old and lives with her mother in temporary housing in a damp, overcrowded flat. Her mother works long hours on a zero-hours contract and the family often relies on a food bank. Sienna has missed several immunisation appointments and has been absent from school frequently due to chest infections.

Using your knowledge of life factors, analyse how the life factors Sienna is experiencing are affecting her PIES development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Identifies at least three distinct life factors accurately (e.g. economic/poverty, living environment, access to services). Chains each factor to its PIES impact and links impacts across domains. Consistently references Sienna's specific circumstances throughout.

Secure (5–6): Identifies two or three life factors with clear PIES links. Some chaining between domains. Generally accurate application to Sienna.

Developing (3–4): Accurate points listed but not chained. Life factors and lifestyle choices may be confused. Limited reference to Sienna.

Emerging (1–2): Basic points with little structure or accuracy.

Indicative content:
• Economic factor/poverty: zero-hours contract and food bank reliance → inadequate nutrition → impaired physical growth and brain development (P and I). Financial stress in the home may create an anxious, unsettled atmosphere affecting Sienna's emotional security (E).
• Living environment: damp, overcrowded flat → respiratory illness → physical health impact (P) → school absence → missed learning → falling behind peers intellectually (I) → reduced social contact with classmates (S).
• Access to services: missed immunisation appointments → higher risk of preventable illness (P), which compounds the cycle of school absence. Access to services is limited by the mother's working hours and transport difficulties.
• Chain: poverty → poor housing → chest infections → school absence → intellectual gaps → social isolation → lower self-esteem (E). These factors interact rather than operating in isolation.
• At age 8 (childhood stage), school attendance and peer relationships are particularly important for intellectual and social milestones — disruption at this stage has long-term consequences.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is one of the four purposes of promoting health and well-being?
A) Diagnosing conditions at an early stage
B) Reducing health and social care costs
C) Providing individual treatment plans
D) Increasing access to prescription medication
practice_questions.marks: B) Reducing health and social care costs [1 mark]. Diagnosis, treatment plans and prescription access are clinical activities rather than health promotion purposes.

practice_questions.text: Give two reasons why health promotion is important for the NHS and social care sector.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct reasons (max 2). Acceptable answers: health promotion reduces demand on NHS services by preventing conditions before they develop [1]; health promotion reduces the long-term costs of treating preventable chronic conditions such as type 2 diabetes [1]; raising awareness means conditions are identified and treated earlier, reducing severity and therefore the level of care needed [1]; enabling positive lifestyle choices reduces the number of people who develop conditions linked to modifiable risk factors [1]. Two near-identical points score 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by a 'strengths-based approach' to supporting individuals to improve their health.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core meaning (identifying and building on the individual's existing strengths, capabilities and resources rather than focusing on deficits); 1 mark for a developed reason using 'because' (e.g. because individuals are more likely to sustain behaviour change when they feel capable and are using resources they already have); 1 mark for a specific practical example (e.g. a health worker asks a service user what has helped them manage their health successfully in the past and encourages them to use those same strategies rather than relying solely on professional support).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a GP surgery could use two different strategies to support patients to take responsibility for their own health and well-being.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks per strategy, applied to the GP surgery context. Education through information and advice (2 marks): 1 mark for naming the strategy; 1 mark for a specific GP surgery example (e.g. the practice provides patients with written information and a referral to an online health programme about managing pre-diabetes, giving them the knowledge and tools to make dietary and exercise changes). Encouraging use of personal strengths and informal networks (2 marks): 1 mark for naming the strategy; 1 mark for a specific example (e.g. the GP asks the patient who in their household or friendship group could walk with them regularly, helping them identify a support network that already exists rather than referring them to a paid service). Prevention and control also accepted with equivalent development.

practice_questions.text:
Sanjay is 52 years old and works in a call centre. He was recently told his blood pressure is borderline high and his BMI is 28.1. His GP wants to support him to make lifestyle changes rather than immediately prescribing medication.

Discuss how the GP could use health promotion strategies to support Sanjay to take responsibility for his own health.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Addresses at least two health promotion strategies with developed reasoning, both linked to Sanjay's specific circumstances (borderline hypertension, overweight BMI, sedentary call-centre job). Education (Sanjay needs information about the link between his lifestyle and his readings, in a format he can act on — because without understanding the connection, he is unlikely to change); strengths-based (asking Sanjay what he enjoys and what small changes he feels able to make builds on his agency rather than imposing a plan); prevention and control (teaching Sanjay to monitor his own blood pressure at home gives him a tool to track his own progress). Considers challenges: Sanjay's sedentary work and possibly limited time for exercise. Uses 'because' and 'therefore'.

Secure (3–4 marks): Addresses at least one strategy with development and some reference to Sanjay.

Developing (2 marks): Names a strategy but limited development; limited link to Sanjay.

Emerging (1 mark): Names a strategy with no development.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the extent to which raising awareness through national health campaigns is an effective strategy for promoting health and well-being across the population.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9–10 marks): Balanced evaluation of national campaigns as a health promotion strategy. Strengths: reach — a well-resourced national campaign (e.g. NHS Better Health) can reach millions of people through television, social media and GP signposting, a scale no individual practitioner can match; they raise awareness across the population, meaning even people who do not access health services may be reached; they normalise health-seeking behaviour and positive lifestyle choices. Limitations: awareness does not guarantee behaviour change — knowing that exercise is good does not mean people exercise more; campaigns may not reach the most deprived communities who face structural barriers to health (cost, access, time, housing); they may be more effective for already-motivated individuals and less so for those who need more personalised support. Comparison: campaigns are more effective when combined with local delivery, individual education and strengths-based approaches — the evidence shows that population-level messaging plus individual support is more effective than either alone. Conclusion: national campaigns are a valuable and necessary component of health promotion but are insufficient on their own; their effectiveness is maximised when they are integrated with local and individual-level support.

Secure (6–8 marks): Addresses most strengths and limitations with some development and a conclusion.

Developing (3–5 marks): Notes some strengths and limitations; limited conclusion.

Emerging (1–2 marks): One-sided or very brief response.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a named UK campaign that promotes awareness of mental health?
A) Dry January
B) Movember
C) Time to Talk Day
D) No Smoking Day
practice_questions.marks: C) Time to Talk Day [1 mark]. Dry January promotes alcohol reduction; Movember promotes men's physical and mental health (accept Movember if a student argues the mental health element, but Time to Talk is the primary mental health campaign listed in the specification); No Smoking Day promotes smoking cessation.

practice_questions.text: Identify two methods that health campaigns use to reach their target audiences.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct methods from the six (max 2). Acceptable answers: printed materials such as leaflets and posters [1]; websites and online resources [1]; television advertisements [1]; celebrities, soap operas and drama [1]; social media and internet pop-ups [1]; guest speakers in schools and colleges [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain why social media is used as a method of delivering health campaigns to young people.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the reason (young people use social media frequently / it reaches a large proportion of the target group); 1 mark for a developed reason using 'because' (e.g. because social media platforms allow campaigns to target specific age groups with relevant, shareable content that can spread peer to peer); 1 mark for a limitation or further development (e.g. however, misinformation also spreads rapidly on social media, so campaign messages from credible NHS or charity sources may compete with inaccurate information from unverified accounts).

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'Five Ways to Well-being' and explain one way in which a health professional could use this framework with a service user.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for accurately describing Five Ways to Well-being (a framework developed by the New Economics Foundation identifying five evidence-based actions to improve well-being: connect, be active, take notice, keep learning, and give [1]; adopted by NHS and public health bodies as a well-being promotion tool [1]). Up to 2 marks for a specific, plausible practitioner example (e.g. a community nurse working with an isolated older adult could use the 'connect' action to encourage them to join a local social group, because social connection is an evidence-based way to improve mental well-being and reduce loneliness [1]; the nurse discusses which of the five actions the service user finds most realistic given their circumstances, applying the framework in a person-centred way [1]).

practice_questions.text:
Devika is 45 years old and is looking for information online about whether she should take a particular herbal supplement that claims to reduce blood pressure. She has found two sources: one from the NHS website and one from a blog run by the supplement manufacturer.

Discuss how Devika could assess the reliability and validity of each source of information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Applies reliability and validity criteria specifically to both sources with developed reasoning. NHS website: produced by a public health body with no commercial interest in a particular product [1]; information is based on clinical evidence reviewed by medical professionals [1]; content is regularly updated, so advice reflects current guidance [1]. Supplement manufacturer's blog: commercial interest — the producer benefits financially from promoting the supplement [1]; evidence may be based on customer testimonials rather than clinical trials, which is less reliable [1]; information may not be reviewed by qualified health professionals and may be out of date or selectively presented [1]. Overall assessment: Devika should rely on the NHS source for accurate guidance on managing blood pressure; the manufacturer's source is less valid because it may not accurately reflect the full clinical picture [1].

Secure (3–4 marks): Addresses both sources with some reliability/validity analysis; at least two developed points.

Developing (2 marks): Addresses one source or gives a very general answer about reliability.

Emerging (1 mark): Identifies one source as more reliable without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how effectively the method of using celebrities and soap opera storylines promotes health and well-being across different groups in the population.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9–10 marks): Balanced evaluation addressing specific strengths and limitations of using celebrities and soap opera storylines as a campaign delivery method, with reference to different population groups. Strengths: reaches large audiences who do not actively seek health information — soap opera viewers include older adults, families and young people across social backgrounds; emotional storytelling can change attitudes more effectively than information alone because audiences empathise with characters; a celebrity speaking openly about mental health (e.g. a public figure discussing depression) can normalise help-seeking, particularly among groups (e.g. men) who are reluctant to admit vulnerability; evidence from mental health charities shows that soap opera storylines (e.g. suicide storylines handled responsibly) lead to increased calls to support services in the following days. Limitations: not always factually accurate — entertainment takes precedence over precision; not all groups watch television or follow specific celebrities — younger people, recent migrants and those without mainstream media access may not be reached; messages delivered indirectly through storylines may not be specific enough to enable individual action; celebrities who endorse products commercially may reduce public trust. Evaluation of effectiveness by group: effective for older adults (high soap viewing rates) and for reducing stigma around mental health (Time to Talk); less effective for reaching those not represented in mainstream media. Conclusion: celebrity and soap methods are effective for reaching broad audiences and changing attitudes, but they should be combined with targeted local delivery methods (e.g. guest speakers, social media) to reach groups underserved by mainstream media.

Secure (6–8 marks): Addresses most strengths and limitations with some group differentiation and a conclusion.

Developing (3–5 marks): Addresses some strengths and limitations; limited differentiation by group.

Emerging (1–2 marks): One-sided or very general response.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is an example of an unexpected life event?
A) Starting secondary school
B) Getting married
C) Retirement
D) Redundancy
practice_questions.marks: D) Redundancy [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two types of physical activity named in the specification.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for any two of the three named types:
• Aerobic activity (1)
• Muscle-strengthening activity (1)
• Bone-strengthening activity (1)
Do not credit generic answers such as 'exercise' or 'sport' without the specific category name.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between binge drinking and alcohol dependence.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
• Binge drinking is consuming a large quantity of alcohol in a single session (1) — for example, 8 or more units for men in one sitting — without a physiological need to do so (1).
• Alcohol dependence is when the body has adapted to require alcohol to function (1), so that stopping causes physical withdrawal symptoms — it is an addiction, not just a pattern of heavy drinking (1).
Award up to 3 marks for clear distinction with developed explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe, with an example, how bereavement as an unexpected life event can affect an individual's emotional and social development.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. 2 marks for emotional; 2 marks for social, each with applied example.
• Emotionally, bereavement can cause grief, guilt, and depression (1) — for example, an adult who loses their spouse may experience persistent low mood and reduced motivation, affecting their ability to manage daily tasks (1).
• Socially, the bereaved individual may withdraw from activities and relationships (1) — for example, stopping attending a weekly club or community group because they feel unable to engage socially, reducing their social support network at a time when it is most needed (1).

practice_questions.text:
Kalani Ferreira is 16 years old and lives with her mother, who was recently diagnosed with a serious mental health condition. Kalani has become her mother's main carer after school and at weekends. She has started skipping meals to save money for the household and has given up her place in a dance group she attended three times a week. She has recently started smoking with some older friends.

Discuss how Kalani's life factors, lifestyle choices, and life events are interrelating to affect her PIES development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Identifies at least one life factor, one lifestyle choice, and one life event from Kalani's scenario. Discusses how they interact with each other and chains the combined impact across multiple PIES domains. Consistently references Kalani's specific circumstances.

Secure (3–4): Identifies relevant factors and choices with some PIES impact. Some interrelation shown. May not fully chain across all three categories.

Developing (2): Accurate identification of factors but treated separately without interrelation. Limited reference to Kalani.

Emerging (1): Basic points, little structure.

Indicative content:
• Life factor: mother's mental health condition — Kalani has become an unexpected young carer (life event). This is also an unexpected life event (significant change in family health).
• Lifestyle choice: skipping meals (poor nutrition) → physical health impact, reduced energy, impaired concentration (P and I). Giving up dance → loss of aerobic and bone-strengthening activity → physical health decline, loss of emotional wellbeing benefit, loss of social group (P, E, S).
• Lifestyle choice: smoking → physical health damage (P), may be a coping mechanism for emotional stress (E).
• Interrelation: the life factor (mother's illness) created a life event (becoming a carer) that constrained Kalani's lifestyle choices (no time for dance, less money for food) and created emotional pressures (worry, isolation from peers) that increased the likelihood of adopting negative lifestyle choices (smoking) as a coping mechanism.
• At 16, adolescence is a critical period for identity formation and peer relationships — being unable to participate in normal adolescent social activities further isolates Kalani.

practice_questions.text:
Devlin Oakes is 58 years old. He was made redundant six months ago after 20 years in the same job. Since losing his job he has been drinking heavily most evenings, rarely leaves the house, and has stopped attending the weekly walking group he used to enjoy. He eats convenience food most days and has put on noticeable weight. His GP has noted elevated blood pressure at a recent check-up.

Using the PIES framework, analyse how Devlin's lifestyle choices and the life event of redundancy are interrelating to affect his health and well-being.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8): Detailed PIES analysis chaining redundancy (unexpected life event) to changes in lifestyle choices, with clear chains of consequence across all four domains. Sustained reference to Devlin's specific circumstances throughout.

Secure (5–6): Clear PIES coverage with accurate analysis of at least three domains. Some chaining between domains. Generally applied to Devlin.

Developing (3–4): Accurate points about PIES and lifestyle choices but listed rather than chained. Limited development or reference to Devlin.

Emerging (1–2): Basic points with little PIES structure.

Indicative content:
• Life event → lifestyle chain: redundancy (unexpected life event) removed Devlin's daily structure, identity, and social contacts from work → triggered increased alcohol consumption (lifestyle choice) as a coping mechanism → elevated blood pressure (P) → increased risk of cardiovascular disease.
• Physical: heavy drinking damages the liver and cardiovascular system; weight gain and elevated blood pressure increase risk of heart disease; loss of aerobic activity (walking group) means reduced cardiovascular fitness and reduced calorie expenditure, compounding weight gain.
• Intellectual: alcohol impairs concentration and decision-making; inactivity reduces cognitive stimulation. At 58 (adulthood), loss of intellectual engagement from work also removes a key source of mental stimulation.
• Emotional: redundancy causes loss of identity, purpose, and routine — significant emotional impact at 58, when career often forms a central part of self-concept. Heavy drinking is a depressant and worsens mood over time, creating a negative cycle.
• Social: stopping the walking group removes his main social contact outside work. Drinking at home isolates him further. Social withdrawal compounds emotional deterioration.
• Interrelation: the life event (redundancy) directly triggered the lifestyle changes (drinking, inactivity, poor diet) by removing structure, purpose, and social contact. These lifestyle changes then produced PIES consequences that compound each other — social isolation worsens emotional wellbeing, which reduces motivation to improve lifestyle, which further harms physical health.

before.exam_tip_html: The key examiner tip for this topic is the interrelation requirement. For 6-, 8-, or 10-mark questions, the mark scheme rewards candidates who show how life factors, lifestyle choices, and life events work together to affect PIES — not who lists them separately. Use a chaining scaffold: “Because of [life factor], the individual was more likely to make [lifestyle choice], which then [PIES impact] — and when [life event] occurred, this was further complicated by …” Also: the spec distinguishes binge drinking from alcohol abuse from alcohol dependence — use the correct term for the stimulus you are given. A common error is calling any heavy drinking “dependence” when the scenario only describes a single session or a recent bereavement.

practice_questions.text:
Which allied health professional specialises in supporting individuals with delayed language development or communication difficulties after a stroke?
A) Occupational therapist
B) Physiotherapist
C) Speech and language therapist
D) District nurse
practice_questions.marks: C) Speech and language therapist [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one difference between formal care and informal care.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for a clear distinction:
• Formal care is provided by trained, paid professionals within organisations; informal care is provided by unpaid individuals such as family members or friends (1).

practice_questions.text: Give two ways that financial support helps individuals who have not reached expected developmental milestones.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for two distinct ways:
• Covers the cost of specialist equipment (mobility aids, hearing aids, adapted tools) that the individual could not otherwise afford (1)
• Allows an informal carer to reduce their working hours to provide care, through Carers' Allowance (1)
• Enables access to therapies (e.g. speech therapy) that would otherwise be unaffordable (1)
• Carers' Allowance helps prevent carers falling into poverty due to their caring role (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how an advocate can support an older adult with dementia who is moving into residential care.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
• An advocate speaks up for the individual's rights and preferences when they cannot effectively do so themselves (1).
• For an older adult with dementia, this is particularly important because the condition may impair their ability to communicate their wishes about their care plan (1).
• Therefore an advocate ensures the care home staff understand the individual's preferences (e.g. meal choices, daily routines, preferred social activities), supporting their emotional wellbeing and sense of identity (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe, with examples from a named care setting, how formal and informal care work together to support a child with a learning disability who has not reached expected intellectual and social milestones.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. 2 marks for formal care with setting-linked example; 2 marks for informal care with complementary example.
• Formal care: in a specialist primary school or children's centre, an educational psychologist and teaching assistant work together to assess the child's needs and provide adapted learning activities that build on their current level (1). A speech and language therapist may provide targeted sessions to support communication development (1).
• Informal care: at home, the child's parents use techniques modelled by the therapist — for example, practising Makaton signing during daily routines (1) — providing consistent reinforcement that extends the benefit of formal therapy into the child's home environment (1).

practice_questions.text:
Marcus Griffiths is 68 years old. He was recently discharged from hospital following a stroke that has left him with weakness on his left side and significant communication difficulties. He lives with his daughter Seren, who works part-time. Marcus finds it hard to express his care preferences to professionals. The local authority has arranged a care package.

Using your knowledge of formal and informal support, evaluate how different types of support could help Marcus meet his developmental needs following the stroke.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9–10): Comprehensive evaluation covering formal care (named professionals with specific functions), informal care (Seren's role, its limitations), advocacy, equipment, financial support, and at least one other support type. Reaches a reasoned overall judgement about the balance and limitations of support. Consistently applied to Marcus's circumstances throughout.

Secure (7–8): Good coverage of formal and informal care with some named professionals and applied examples. Addresses at least three support types. Some evaluative comment but may not balance positive and limitations or reach a clear judgement.

Developing (4–6): Accurate content but may list types without evaluating. May not address the limitation of Seren as informal carer or acknowledge potential gaps in provision.

Emerging (1–3): Basic points. Limited application to Marcus.

Indicative content:
Formal care:
• Physiotherapist: supports rehabilitation of left-side weakness through targeted exercises — directly addresses physical developmental need (P).
• Speech and language therapist: supports Marcus's communication difficulties, enabling him to express needs and preferences — critical given his communication barriers (I and E).
• GP and district nurse: ongoing monitoring of health and medication; coordinating further referrals if needed.
• Occupational therapist: assesses and adapts Marcus's home environment (e.g. grab rails, adapted kitchen equipment) to support independence in later adulthood.

Informal care:
• Seren provides daily personal care and emotional support — essential but demanding. Her part-time work limits availability; without respite care, she risks carer burnout which would reduce the quality of support Marcus receives.
• Respite care or a carers' assessment would identify Seren's own needs and provide formal breaks.

Advocacy:
• Marcus's communication difficulty means he struggles to express care preferences. A professional advocate ensures his wishes are represented in care planning meetings — supporting his right to person-centred care and his emotional wellbeing and sense of control.

Equipment and financial support:
• Mobility aids (walking frame, wheelchair) and home adaptations (wet room, raised toilet) support physical independence. These may be funded through Attendance Allowance or a local authority community care grant.
• Personal Independence Payment may supplement income if Marcus can no longer work.

Support groups:
• A stroke survivors' group provides social contact, information from others who have recovered, and emotional validation — reducing isolation.

Evaluation / judgement:
• Formal and informal care together are more effective than either alone — therapy is only beneficial if supported by consistent practice at home. However, the burden on Seren is significant and sustainable only with respite and financial support. The advocacy role is particularly important for Marcus given his communication difficulty — without it, his formal care risks being planned without his input, reducing its effectiveness and his sense of dignity and control.
